newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK M4 to show flourishing consumer demand.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK M4 to show flourishing consumer demand.

text.p: British broad money supply data will reflect an economy that was still bubbling in March and consumers who are showing no reluctance to borrow, economists said on Wednesday.
M4 money and lending data will be released at 0830 GMT on Friday. A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus expecting M4 growth of 11.0 percent year-on-year and a 0.8 percent rise from February.
M4 lending is forecast to rise by 6.1 billion pounds, having shot up by 8.2 billion in February.
"Credit growth continues to fuel the rise in M4," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell . He forecast a 5.5 billion stg increase in M4 lending in March.

The government has imposed a three-to-nine percent monitoring range for M4, but the broad money supply measure has rarely dipped below the upper level in recent months. In February, M4 leapt by 1.4 percent from the month before, putting it 11.2 percent higher than a year earlier.
"Both money and credit growth have remained strong in recent months," said Michael Saunders, Salomon Brothers' UK economist.

M4 measures all bank and building society deposits, both corporate and personal, together with cash held by the public and the entire stock of household mortgage debt. Saunders said M4's strength may partly reflect heavy issuance of sterling eurobonds in recent months.

"Overseas residents seem to have borrowed sterling to buy these issues and the issuers of these securities have, as a result, received extra funds which count towards M4," he said. But essentially, a sharply growing broad money supply measure reflects buoyant consumer demand.

Economists at Julius Baer Investments said low interest rates, falling unemployment, rising house prices and the prospect of 21 billion stg in windfall payments from building societies converting into banks all added up to buoyant high street conditions.
"Consumer confidence is back to levels last seen at the height of the late-1980s boom," they said.
At the same time as the Bank of England unveils its latest M4 data, the Building Societies Association will release figures showing how much money was lent in new mortgages last month.
The Reuter poll forecasts net new approvals totalled a seasonally adjusted 3.1 billion stg in March, just below February's 3.4 billion.

"Although there are some indications that the acceleration in mortgage borrowing has eased back lately, this is being offset by buoyant credit demand," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.

He said looming May Day elections may have put a cap on house buying activity for a little while. Some economists think shadow Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will push up interest rates quickly if Labour takes power, to establish his anti-inflationary credentials.
Labour, about 20 points ahead in the polls, is poised to take power for the first time since 1979.

But the tail-off in mortgage activity could just as easily reflect the chronic shortage of houses coming onto the market -- that lack of supply has been largely responsible for pushing prices sharply higher.

"Total net advances, the annual growth of mortgage approvals, transactions and housing starts have all edged back," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe. "House prices...continue to rise strongly reflecting a limited supply of property."
